title: Doing the work in order
objectives: Order a graph's nodes topologically and run the backward pass in the reverse order.

screens.title: The wrong order
screens.prose: Back to $g = (x + y)x$ with every gradient at 0. Sam runs the sum box's backward step first, then the product box's. When the sum box runs, $\partial g/\partial s$ is still 0.
screens.question: What does Sam's run leave in `y.grad`?

hints.text: What does the sum box pass on when its own gradient is still 0?
It passes $0 \times 1$ to $y$.
The product box runs later, but nothing sends $y$ anything after that.

feedback.correct: `y.grad` stays 0: the sum box passed on a gradient that was not ready yet.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What did $s$ hold when its box ran?

byKey.right-order: That is the right gradient, but Sam's sum box ran while $\partial g/\partial s$ was still 0.

explain.text: The sum box ran before the product box had sent it anything, so it passed 0 to $y$. A box must wait until every box after it has run.

screens.title: Topological order
screens.prose: A list in which every node comes after the nodes that feed it is in **topological order**. The forward pass runs in such an order. The backward pass runs in the **reverse** order, so each box is done only after every box it feeds.
screens.question: Put the seven nodes of the course graph in a topological order. Any valid order is accepted.

hints.text: Leaves first: nothing feeds them.
$e$ needs $a$ and $b$; $d$ needs $e$ and $c$.
For example $a, b, e, c, d, f, L$.

feedback.correct: Every node sits after the nodes that feed it. Read backwards, it is the order of the backward pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A node must come after every node with an arrow into it.

byKey.e: $e$ came before one of its inputs, $a$ or $b$.
byKey.d: $d$ came before one of its inputs, $e$ or $c$.

explain.text: Any order with $e$ after $a$ and $b$, $d$ after $e$ and $c$, and $L$ after $d$ and $f$ is topological. The backward pass reads such a list from the end.

screens.title: Building the order by search
screens.question: Slide through the search. Which node is appended fifth?

options.why: $c$ is fourth: $d$ visits $e$ first, then $c$, then appends itself.
$f$ is a parent of $L$, visited after $d$ is finished: it is sixth.
$L$ is appended last, after both its parents.

hints.text: Step the slider and read the list.
The list grows $a, b, e, c, \ldots$
Fifth comes $d$, once $e$ and $c$ are in.

feedback.correct: $a, b, e, c, d, f, L$: $d$ is fifth, after both its parents.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the fifth cell of the list.

explain.text: The search finishes a node only after all its parents, so the list is $a, b, e, c, d, f, L$. Read from the end, it is the backward order.

screens.title: Seven nodes, two branches
screens.prose: A graph of seven nodes: $k = uv$, $m = k + w$, $n = mu$, $o = n + v$, at $u = 2$, $v = -1$, $w = 3$. Both $u$ and $v$ are used twice. Run the backward pass in reverse topological order: $o, n, m, k$, then the leaves.
screens.question: Fill in each gradient.

hints.text: Work in the order $o, n, m, k$, adding into $u$ and $v$ as you go.
$n$ gets 1; $m$ gets $1 \times u = 2$; $u$ gets $1 \times m = 1$ from $n$.
$k$ and $w$ get 2; then $u$ gets $2 \times v = -2$ more and $v$ gets $2 \times u = 4$ more.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each node adds what every box it feeds sends back.

byKey.one-path-u: You kept only the path through $k$. The box $n = mu$ also sends $u$ the value $m = 1$.
byKey.other-path-u: You kept only the path through $n$. The path through $k$ adds $-2$.
byKey.one-path-v: You kept only the path through $k$. $v$ also goes straight into $o$, which adds 1.
byKey.direct-v: You kept only the direct arrow into $o$. The path through $k$ adds 4.
byKey.used-m: You used $m$ itself. The product $n = mu$ passes $m$ the other input, $u = 2$.

explain.text: In reverse order: $n$ gets 1, $m$ gets $u = 2$, $k$ and $w$ get 2. $u$ collects $m = 1$ from $n$ and $2v = -2$ from $k$, so $-1$; $v$ collects 1 from $o$ and $2u = 4$ from $k$, so 5.

screens.title: Every node ever made
screens.prose: Sam keeps a list of every node his script has ever made, and runs the backward pass over it in reverse creation order. An old node $p = 3w$ from an earlier pass still holds `p.grad = 1`. Now he builds $L = 5w$, zeroes `w.grad` and runs his backward pass from $L$.
screens.question: What should `w.grad` be after a correct backward pass from $L$?

hints.text: Which nodes lie on a path from $w$ to $L$?
Only the box $L = 5w$. The old node $p$ does not lead to $L$.
So $\partial L/\partial w = 5$.

feedback.correct: Only $L = 5w$ lies on the way to $L$, so `w.grad` should be 5. Sam's list adds the stale 3 and gives 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use only the nodes that lead to $L$.

byKey.stale: That is what Sam's list gives: the old node $p$ adds its stale $3 \times 1$. It is not part of this graph.
byKey.old: That came from the old node $p$, which does not lead to $L$.

explain.text: A topological order built from $L$ holds only the nodes that lead to $L$, so `w.grad` should be 5. Sam's list of everything also ran the old $p$, which added a stale 3 into `w.grad`.

screens.title: A node that does not lead to the output
screens.prose: The course script also computes $t = 3z$, which nothing uses. The search `build(L)` starts from $L$ and follows parents only.
screens.question: How many nodes does `build(L)` put in the list?

hints.text: The search follows arrows backwards from $L$.
No arrow leads from $t$ or $z$ to $L$.
It finds $a, b, c, f, e, d, L$.

feedback.correct: Seven: $z$ and $t$ are never reached, so their gradients stay 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count what the search reaches from $L$.

byKey.all: You counted $z$ and $t$. The search never reaches them from $L$.
byKey.ops: You counted the boxes only. The leaves are nodes too.

explain.text: Searching back from $L$ reaches the 7 nodes of the course graph and nothing else. $z$ and $t$ are left out, and their gradients stay 0.

screens.title: Topological order in code
screens.prose: A graph arrives as a dict from each node's name to the list of names that feed it: the course graph is `{"L": ["d", "f"], "d": ["e", "c"], "e": ["a", "b"], "a": [], ...}`. Write `topo_order(node, parents)`: the nodes that lead to `node`, each after its parents.
screens.question: Write `topo_order(node, parents)`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests on four graphs: the course graph, a diamond, the seven-node graph and the course graph with an unused node. A checker accepts any valid order; it must hold exactly the nodes that lead to the root.

hints.text: Write the recursive search from the last screen, with `parents[v]` in place of `v._prev`.
Keep a `seen` set so a node shared by two paths is added once.
Append `v` after the loop over its parents.

feedback.correct: The search appends each node after all its parents, once, and reaches only what leads to the root.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is a diamond: `x` feeds both `left` and `right`. Without a `seen` set, `x` appears twice.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has a node `t` that does not lead to `L`. Search from the root only.

explain.text: `build(v)` finishes every parent before appending `v`, and `seen` stops a shared node from being added twice. Starting at the root, it never meets a node that does not lead there.

screens.title: The backward pass in order
screens.prose:
The backward pass is three steps:
```python
topo = topological order from the output
output.grad = 1
for v in reversed(topo):
    v._backward()
```
Reversed, every box runs after all the boxes it feeds, so its gradient is complete when it passes it on.
screens.question: Why is the order reversed?

options.text: A box must collect every contribution before it passes its gradient back
So the leaves are processed first, before any box
options.why: Reversed, the leaves come last. The output comes first.

options.text: Reversed lists run faster in Python than forward ones
options.why: Speed is not the reason. The order decides whether each gradient is complete.

options.text: So the forward pass is repeated on the way back
options.why: The forward pass is already done. The backward pass only reads its values.

hints.text: Remember Sam's first run.
The sum box ran before anything had reached it.
Reverse order means every later box has already sent its share.

feedback.correct: In reverse order, every box that a node feeds has already run.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think of the box that ran too early.

explain.text: A node's gradient collects a share from every box it feeds. In reverse topological order those boxes have all run, so the gradient is complete before it is passed on.

screens.title: A pricing library
screens.prose: A swap pricer runs its steps in the same kind of order as a build system: nothing runs before its inputs exist. A risk run then walks the same list backwards to get the PV's sensitivity to each quote.
screens.question: Put the pricing steps in an order the library can run. Either order of the two middle steps is accepted.

lines.text: Swap PV (needs discount factors and forward rates)

hints.text: Start with what needs nothing.
The curve needs the quotes; both discount factors and forwards need the curve.
Quotes, curve, then the two in either order, then the PV.

feedback.correct: A topological order: each step after what it needs. The risk run reads it backwards.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each step must come after every step it needs.

byKey.cv: The curve came before the quotes it is fitted to.
byKey.df: Discount factors came before the curve.
byKey.fw: Forward rates came before the curve.
byKey.pv: The PV came before one of its inputs.

explain.text: The pricer computes in a topological order, like a build system or the forward pass. The risk run walks it backwards, as backpropagation does, so each sensitivity is complete before it is passed on.

ideas: In a topological order every node comes after the nodes that feed it.
A search from the output that appends each node after its parents builds such an order, and only of nodes that lead to the output.
The backward pass runs the order reversed, so each gradient is complete before it is passed on.

formula.name: Backward pass
formula.note: A box runs only after every box it feeds.

summary.trap: A list of every node ever made can hold old nodes that do not lead to the output; their stale gradients leak in.

quiz.prose: A graph's topological order is $p, q, r, s, t$, with $t$ the output.
quiz.question: Which node does the backward pass process first?

options.why: You read the list forwards. The backward pass reads it from the end.
Those are leaves; they come last backwards.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The backward pass starts at the output.

explain.text: The backward pass runs the reversed list, so it starts at the output $t$ with gradient 1.

quiz.prose: In a graph, $m$ feeds $n$, $n$ feeds $o$, and $k$ feeds $o$.
quiz.question: Which list is in topological order?

options.why: That is reversed: the output comes first.

feedback.correct: $k, m, n, o$: every node after what feeds it.

explain.text: $m$ before $n$, $n$ before $o$ and $k$ before $o$ all hold in $k, m, n, o$.

quiz.prose: A script builds a graph with output $L$, and also a node $u$ that nothing on the way to $L$ uses.
quiz.question: What happens to $u$ in `L.backward()`?

options.text: It is not in the order, and its gradient stays 0
The backward pass raises an error
options.why: Nothing breaks: the search simply never reaches $u$.

options.text: It gets gradient 1, like the output
It keeps whatever gradient it had and passes it on
options.why: It is never processed, so it passes nothing on.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Where does the search start?

explain.text: The order is built by searching back from $L$. $u$ does not lead to $L$, so it is never added and its gradient stays 0.
